title: The Window Washer's Son: Cicero to the Tower of Nicholas V
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Cicero, Illinois, born in the Lithuanian quarter
stops.date_confidence: Birth date, city and family attested (Wikipedia, 'Paul Marcinkus'; lithaz.org biography). The parish is [R]: no source consulted names the family's own parish or street address, and St. Anthony of Padua stands here only as the Lithuanian parish of Cicero. Coordinates set to 1515 S 50th Ave, correcting a value in the research pool that fell 1.4 km southwest of the church.
stops.campa: In the Lithuanian quarter of Cicero, west of Chicago's stockyards, Paul Casimir Marcinkus is born the youngest of five children. His father washes windows for a living; his mother works in a bakery. The parish that anchors the neighborhood is St. Anthony of Padua, raised by immigrants who crossed an ocean to work the factories of Illinois. He grows up big and easy with people, in a town whose name in the 1920s means Al Capone to the rest of America. Which parish the family actually kept, and on what street they lived, no record consulted says.
suggested_refs: St. Anthony of Padua parish, 1515 S 50th Ave, Cicero, the Lithuanian parish of the neighborhood

stops.name: Mundelein, the seminary of St. Mary of the Lake
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The seminary years are given by lithaz.org and repeated by Wikipedia without dates; c. 1938-1943 is the ordinary Chicago sequence for a 1947 ordination, not a documented enrollment record. Month and day defaulted to 01. Physical details of the campus are general, not drawn from any account of Marcinkus's own residence there.
stops.campa: The seminary of St. Mary of the Lake stands forty miles north of the city on its own lake: Georgian brick and white columns, raised by Cardinal Mundelein, who wanted his priests trained in something that looked like Virginia rather than like the Back of the Yards. What his classmates remember afterward is not a scholar but an organizer, the one who arranges things and knows whom to ask. Marcinkus reads philosophy and theology here through the war years. He grows to six feet three.
suggested_refs: The University of St. Mary of the Lake, Mundelein, seminary of the Archdiocese of Chicago

stops.name: Chicago, ordained a priest of the archdiocese
stops.date_confidence: Date, archdiocese and ordaining prelate attested (Wikipedia, 'Paul Marcinkus'; catholic-hierarchy.org). The VENUE is [R] and the sources conflict with the pin: no source located places the ordination at Holy Name Cathedral, and Chicago ordinations of that era were customarily held in the seminary chapel at Mundelein. The cathedral pin is used because he is buried from it in 2006; the contradiction is flagged, not resolved. Coordinates corrected to 735 N State St.
stops.campa: Cardinal Samuel Stritch ordains him a priest of the Archdiocese of Chicago on the third of May, 1947, at twenty-five. He has no money of his own and no training in the handling of anyone else's. The archdiocese is at its high-water mark: a city of parishes where the Church runs schools, hospitals, courts of its own, and the politics of whole wards. He is assigned to parish work on the South Side, among people who speak his parents' language, and says his first Masses in a neighborhood of two-flats and packinghouse shifts.
suggested_refs: Cardinal Samuel Stritch, Archbishop of Chicago 1939-1958, ordaining prelate

stops.name: Back of the Yards, the parishes and the tribunal
stops.date_confidence: Parish assignments at St. Christina's and Holy Cross and the 1949 appointment to the archdiocesan matrimonial tribunal are attested (Wikipedia, 'Paul Marcinkus'). Month and day defaulted to 01. Coordinates corrected to 4557 S Wood St; the value in the research pool sat 1.5 km north and duplicated a latitude used for St. Casimir Cemetery, evidently a copying error.
stops.campa: Assistant pastor at St. Christina's, then at Holy Cross in Back of the Yards, a Lithuanian parish standing among the packinghouses where the language is still preached from the pulpit. Within two years the archdiocese moves him to the matrimonial tribunal, the court that hears petitions for annulment. The young priest finds he has a head for procedure and for the exact wording of a canon. It is administrative work rather than pastoral work, and he does it for four years before Rome sends for him.
suggested_refs: The matrimonial tribunal of the Archdiocese of Chicago, to which he was appointed in 1949

stops.name: Rome, canon law and the school for nuncios
stops.date_confidence: The credential is contradicted between sources and the contradiction is left open. Wikipedia specifies a degree in canon law and the program of the Pontifical Ecclesiastical Academy; the deep-research dossier gives a doctorate from the Pontifical Gregorian University. Both are reported here. The pin is the Gregorian, on Piazza della Pilotta. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He is sent to Rome for canon law and for the training that produces Vatican diplomats. The sources disagree on the credential: some biographies give him a doctorate from the Pontifical Gregorian University, the Jesuit school that stocks the Curia; the standard reference specifies the course of the Pontifical Ecclesiastical Academy, the Holy See's own school for its own foreign service. Either way a Chicago parish priest comes out of it an officer of a diplomatic corps older than most of the states it deals with. Which of the two lecture halls he actually sat in has never been settled.
suggested_refs: The Pontifical Ecclesiastical Academy, Piazza della Minerva, training school of the papal diplomatic service

stops.name: La Paz, secretary at the nunciature
stops.date_confidence: Posting and dates attested at city level (Wikipedia, 'Paul Marcinkus'; Grokipedia chronology). The nunciature building's own coordinates are [R]: city-level pin only. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Posted as secretary to the apostolic nunciature in Bolivia, three and a half kilometers above the sea, where the Church is the oldest continuous institution in the country and the government is not. He is thirty-three, and has never handled an account larger than a parish collection. He learns Spanish here and keeps it for life. The work is unglamorous: correspondence, visas, the endless courtesies of a mission accredited to a state that changes hands often. The posting runs four years, to 1959.
suggested_refs: The Apostolic Nunciature to Bolivia, La Paz

stops.name: Ottawa, the apostolic delegation
stops.date_confidence: Posting attested (Wikipedia; Grokipedia). The research pool called this a nunciature in one lens and a delegation in another: the delegation is correct, since the Holy See and Canada established full diplomatic relations only in 1969. Coordinates corrected to 724 Manor Ave, Rockcliffe Park; the pool's value sat 5 km south in Alta Vista. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: He is transferred north to the Holy See's mission in Ottawa, a house on Manor Avenue in Rockcliffe Park. Canada and the Vatican have no full diplomatic relations yet, so the post is an apostolic delegation, accredited to the Canadian bishops rather than to the Crown, and the business is church administration rather than statecraft: appointments of bishops, seminary questions, the paperwork of a national hierarchy. There is snow, there is a small staff, and there is no use at all for the Spanish he has just learned. It is the third posting in four years. He stays less than a year.
suggested_refs: The Apostolic Delegation to Canada, 724 Manor Avenue, Rockcliffe Park, Ottawa

stops.name: The Apostolic Palace, into the Secretariat of State
stops.date_confidence: Month and year attested (Wikipedia, 'Paul Marcinkus'); day defaulted to 01. The pin is the Apostolic Palace, inherited from william_casey.journey.json's Vatican pin for the same building. The characterization of the Montini friendship as decisive is the judgment of the biographies, not a documented statement by either man.
stops.campa: In December he enters the Secretariat of State inside the Apostolic Palace, the department that conducts the Holy See's relations with the world and, in practice, conducts the Holy See. Giovanni Battista Montini, Milanese and frail, has already been moved sideways once by the previous pope. Marcinkus is put to English translation and to the logistics of travel: itineraries, aircraft, the order of a receiving line. The biographies date his friendship with the future Paul VI from these rooms, and none of them cites either man saying so.
suggested_refs: The Secretariat of State, Apostolic Palace, Vatican City

stops.name: Via della Nocetta, the founding of Villa Stritch
stops.date_confidence: Founding role attested (americamagazine.org profile: he 'directed the execution' of the founding and kept a room there; comboni2000.org and il Giornale confirm the purchase of two condominiums on Via della Nocetta). Dated to the mid-1960s; exact year not established, month and day defaulted to 01. The extraterritoriality claim carried in the research pool is REJECTED here: Villa Stritch is USCCB property with no Lateran privilege.
stops.campa: He persuades the American bishops to buy two condominium blocks on Via della Nocetta, beside the Villa Pamphili, as a residence for American priests working inside the Roman Curia. It is named Villa Stritch, for the cardinal who ordained him. The house belongs to the bishops' conference of the United States and carries no extraterritorial privilege whatever, whatever is written later about him sheltering there from Italian magistrates. He keeps a room in it for twenty-five years, and a tennis court within reach.
suggested_refs: Villa Stritch, Via della Nocetta 63, Rome, residence for American clergy of the Curia
sources: HuffPost, 'While Pope Francis Lives In A Dorm, U.S. Bishops Enjoy Italian Luxury'
comboni2000.org; il Giornale (Italian reporting on the purchase)

segments.name: The Papon: Bodyguard to Paul VI

stops.name: Vatican City, the pope's English voice
stops.date_confidence: Interpreting for John XXIII and for Paul VI, and the informal bodyguard role on foreign journeys, are attested (Wikipedia, 'Paul Marcinkus'; deep-research dossier). The nickname is reported both ways and both are given: Wikipedia treats 'il Papon' as the nickname tied to the bodyguard role, while 'the Gorilla' is the press epithet (America Magazine, 'The legend of the Pope's Gorilla'). Which came first is not established. Month and day defaulted to 01.
stops.campa: Montini is elected in June and takes the name Paul VI. Marcinkus, who has already interpreted for John XXIII, becomes the pope's English voice and the man who plans his journeys: Jerusalem, Bombay, New York, Bogota. He is six feet three and broad across, and on foreign trips he walks in front, clearing a path through crowds for which no Swiss Guard has been drilled. The Italian press calls him il Papon. The English-language press prefers the Gorilla. Both stick, and the sources disagree about which came first.
suggested_refs: America Magazine, 'The legend of the Pope's Gorilla'
sources: America Magazine, 'The legend of the Pope's Gorilla'

stops.name: The Torrione di Niccolo V, named secretary of the bank
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'Paul Marcinkus'; catholic-hierarchy.org). Pin inherited byte-identical from licio_gelli.journey.json's stop for the Institute for Religious Works, the corpus's canonical pin for this building; the geography lens offered a slightly different value and it is not used, so that all IOR stops in the atlas fall on one point.
stops.campa: On Christmas Eve Paul VI names him secretary of the Institute for the Works of Religion, the bank housed in the Torrione di Niccolo V behind the Apostolic Palace, and Titular Bishop of Horta, a North African see with no flock for a thousand years. The institute takes deposits from religious orders, dioceses and Vatican employees, moves money across borders no other bank can move it across, and answers to nobody outside the walls. Its new secretary has never worked in a bank. He is asked afterward how he came to be given it.
stops.quote: I have no banking experience, but I think I was chosen because of the organizational ability I showed when it was needed during the Pope's travels.
stops.quote_source: Marcinkus, quoted in TIME, 'Scandal at the Pope's Bank' (1982)
suggested_refs: The Torrione di Niccolo V, seat of the Institute for the Works of Religion since 1938

stops.name: St. Peter's Basilica, consecrated bishop
stops.date_confidence: Attested (catholic-hierarchy.org; deep-research dossier timeline). That his mother was or was not present is not recorded in any source consulted; the campa states the absence of record, not an absence of the mother.
stops.campa: On Epiphany, under Bernini's canopy, Paul VI consecrates him bishop in St. Peter's, laying hands on the head of a man he first met as a translator. Marcinkus is forty-six, and twenty-two years out of a South Side parish. From this day he is addressed as Excellency and keeps his American passport, and the institution he answers to the pope for is one whose accounts no auditor outside Vatican City has ever seen. Whether the bakery worker from Cicero is in the basilica that morning, no source records.
suggested_refs: Titular see of Horta, conferred 24 December 1968

stops.name: Manila airport, the knife at the arrival ceremony
stops.date_confidence: Date, place and attacker attested (EWTN Vatican; National Catholic Register, 'The Man Who Saved Two Popes'; America Magazine; contemporaneous UPI wire caption). The research pool tagged this [R] in one lens and [A] in another; the event is [A], and only the identity of who stopped Mendoza is genuinely contested, most accounts crediting Marcinkus and President Ferdinand Marcos claiming publicly that he disabled the man himself. The chalice inscription is quoted from the object's own engraving as reported in the UPI caption.
stops.campa: At the arrival ceremony at Manila airport a Bolivian painter named Benjamin Mendoza y Amor Flores, dressed as a priest, comes at Paul VI with a kris knife. Marcinkus is standing beside the pope and moves. Most accounts credit him with the block; President Ferdinand Marcos will claim publicly that he disabled the attacker himself with a karate chop. Paul VI is unhurt and continues the visit. The chalice used at the Mass the next day is given to the bishop who stood in the way, with the occasion cut into the metal.
stops.quote: Chalice used by Pope Paul VI in ordination in Manila November 28, 1970. Gift of Paul VI to Paul C. Marcinkus by Paul VI.
stops.quote_source: Engraved inscription on the chalice given by Paul VI, reported in the contemporaneous UPI wire photo caption
suggested_refs: National Catholic Register, 'The Man Who Saved Two Popes'
The competing Marcos account of the Manila attack

stops.name: The Institute for the Works of Religion, made president
stops.date_confidence: Appointment attested; the geography lens dates it to October 1971 and the day is defaulted to 01. Wikipedia's statement that he took the post 'at age 48' is arithmetically impossible: born 15 January 1922, he was 49 throughout 1971, and the age is corrected here. The quote is confirmed verbatim in The Irish Times obituary, which prints 'church' in lower case.
stops.campa: At forty-nine he is made president of the Institute for the Works of Religion. The bank occupies a fifteenth-century defensive tower with slit windows and a marble counter, staffed by few enough people to know each other by name, holding accounts for cardinals, for orders of nuns, and, as it will turn out, for other people. He has a bishop's ring, a degree in canon law and no banking qualification of any kind. Asked why a Church needs a bank at all, he answers in one sentence.
stops.quote: You can't run a church on Hail Marys.
stops.quote_source: Marcinkus, quoted in The Irish Times obituary, 'God's Banker and Papal Bodyguard' (February 2006)
suggested_refs: The presidency of the IOR, 1971-1989
sources: The Irish Times, 'God's Banker and Papal Bodyguard' (Feb 2006)

stops.name: Nassau, a bishop on an offshore board
stops.date_confidence: Board membership attested (court-document summary of Banco Ambrosiano deposit operations, fraudauditing.blogspot.com; deep-research dossier; corroborated by licio_gelli.journey.json, which names Marcinkus on the board of Ambrosiano's Nassau subsidiary). The relationship spans roughly 1971-1982; the date here orders the segment and does not mark an event. City-level pin: the office address in Nassau is not confirmed and is [R].
stops.campa: He takes a seat on the board of Cisalpine Overseas Bank in Nassau, set up with the Sicilian financier Michele Sindona and the Milanese banker Roberto Calvi, and flies out for meetings. A bishop of the Roman Church sits on that board because the Roman Church's own bank is in the business with them. The bank is offshore in the full sense: outside Italian exchange controls, outside Italian bank inspection, useful for moving money that would be visible anywhere else. He keeps the seat until 1982.
suggested_refs: Cisalpine Overseas Bank (later Banco Ambrosiano Overseas), Nassau
sources: fraudauditing.blogspot.com, court-document summary of Banco Ambrosiano deposit operations

stops.name: Vatican City, questioned about the counterfeit bonds
stops.date_confidence: Attested (Wikipedia, 'Paul Marcinkus'). The interview was conducted by United States federal prosecutors; Marcinkus was in Vatican City and the stop is pinned there rather than in the United States, since he did not travel to it. No charge followed, and the record does not say what he told them.
stops.campa: United States federal prosecutors want to know about fourteen and a half million dollars in counterfeit American bonds delivered to the Vatican in July 1971. They put their questions to him on the twenty-fourth of April, and he answers them from inside a foreign state where no American subpoena runs. It is the first appearance of his name in an American criminal file, and the first time the words Vatican bank turn up in a wire story about fraud. No charge follows. What he told them, the record does not say.
suggested_refs: The July 1971 delivery of counterfeit bonds to the Vatican, subject of the US federal inquiry

stops.name: Mineola, Long Island, the Franklin National fails
stops.date_confidence: Insolvency date attested (Wikipedia, 'Michele Sindona'; TIME archive). Coordinates corrected to Mineola, where the bank's headquarters stood from 1960 until the failure; the research pool pinned Franklin Square, the village of the bank's origin (liherald.com, 'Rise and fall of Franklin National Bank'). The scale of the Vatican bank's losses is reported as tens of millions and is not precisely established. Marcinkus was not present; the stop is his because the loss is his institution's.
stops.campa: Michele Sindona's American vehicle, the Franklin National Bank of Mineola, is declared insolvent for fraud and currency speculation: the largest bank failure in United States history to that date. In Milan the collapse of Sindona's whole structure is already being called il crack Sindona, and the Vatican bank, in with him, loses tens of millions of dollars. No source puts a figure on the loss. Sindona has been telling people for years what the Vatican connection is worth to him.
stops.quote: We used his name a lot in business deals. I told him clearly that I put him in because it helps me get money.
stops.quote_source: Michele Sindona, quoted in TIME, 'Italy: The Great Vatican Bank Mystery' (1982)
suggested_refs: Michele Sindona's conviction on 65 counts in New York, 1980, and his life sentence in Italy for the murder of the liquidator Giorgio Ambrosoli, 1986
sources: TIME, 'Italy: The Great Vatican Bank Mystery' (1982)
liherald.com, 'Rise and fall of Franklin National Bank'

stops.name: Milan, the priests' bank behind Piazza Paolo Ferrari
stops.date_confidence: The working alliance with Calvi and the IOR's shareholding are attested (Intesa Sanpaolo historical bank archive; Forbes; deep-research dossier); licio_gelli.journey.json independently dates Calvi's chairmanship to 1975, which is the year used here to order the segment. The relationship runs to 1982. Coordinates corrected to Piazza Paolo Ferrari; the pool's value fell some 380 m south near the Duomo. Calvi's P2 membership is attested; no meeting between Marcinkus and Gelli is attested anywhere in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: Banco Ambrosiano, the second private bank of Milan, keeps its headquarters on the block behind Piazza Paolo Ferrari: a Catholic bank founded for Catholic depositors and known in the city as the priests' bank. Its chairman is Roberto Calvi, small and silent behind a chain of cigarettes, a sworn member of Licio Gelli's masonic lodge Propaganda Due. The Vatican bank becomes a shareholder and a partner, and Marcinkus and Calvi build a structure of Panamanian and Luxembourg companies whose ownership runs back inside the walls. No source consulted puts Marcinkus and Gelli in a room together.
suggested_refs: licio_gelli.journey.json, for the P2 lodge and Calvi's membership
The Intesa Sanpaolo historic archive on the Piazza Paolo Ferrari headquarters block
sources: Forbes, 'When The Apparent Suicide Of God's Banker Was Ruled A Murder'

stops.name: Lugano, the accounts at the Banca del Gottardo
stops.date_confidence: Attested from the Tribunale di Roma technical accounting consultancy on the Calvi case (philipwillan.com PDF). The research pool titled this place 'Basel/Banca del Gottardo, Lugano', conflating two cities: the bank was headquartered in Lugano and the Basel prefix is struck. Dated c. 1978-1982; month and day defaulted to 01 to order the segment.
stops.campa: Banca del Gottardo in Lugano, an hour over the Swiss border from Milan, holds the accounts of United Trading Company and the other shells at the center of the structure. Ambrosiano money leaves Italy, arrives in Switzerland, buys Ambrosiano shares through companies no regulator can trace to a person, and comes back as debt. Marcinkus is an administrator of that network, not a clerk in it. Italian investigators reconstructing the flows will need a team of accountants and several volumes to say where the money went. The arrangement runs from about 1978 until the bank fails.
suggested_refs: Tribunale di Roma, technical accounting consultancy on the Calvi case (philipwillan.com)
sources: Tribunale di Roma accounting consultancy, Calvi case (philipwillan.com PDF)

stops.name: Castel Gandolfo, the death of the pope who made him
stops.date_confidence: Paul VI's death at Castel Gandolfo on 6 August 1978 is attested in the standard papal record. Marcinkus's own presence at the villa that evening is NOT attested; the deep-research dossier places him among the inner circle in the days that follow, and the campa claims no more than that.
stops.campa: Paul VI dies at the summer palace above Lake Albano, eighty years old, after Sunday Mass. The pope who found a Chicago translator useful, made him a bishop and handed him the bank is gone, and with him a protection no memorandum ever recorded. Two popes follow within two months, the second of them a Pole who knows nothing of Italian banking and has Poland on his mind. Marcinkus keeps the office through both of them. Where he was himself that August evening, no source says.
suggested_refs: The papal apartments of Castel Gandolfo, where Paul VI died 6 August 1978
sources: standard papal biographical record of Paul VI

stops.name: The Institute for the Works of Religion, the letters of patronage
stops.date_confidence: Corrected date. The letters were signed 1 September 1981, paired with Calvi's counter-letter of 27 August 1981 indemnifying the IOR; the research pool's range of 1982-1984 describes when they were litigated, not when they were issued. His defence that the letters were internal is his own reported account (NYT and Washington Post reporting synthesized in the dossier) and is stated as his claim, not as a finding.
stops.campa: On the first of September he signs letters of patronage: documents on the letterhead of the Institute for the Works of Religion acknowledging that the institute controls the Panamanian companies holding roughly a billion dollars of Ambrosiano debt. Five days earlier Calvi has signed a counter-letter indemnifying the institute against any loss arising from them. Marcinkus maintains to the end of his life that the letters were internal comfort, never meant to leave a drawer, and that Calvi broke the arrangement by showing them to creditors.
suggested_refs: Calvi's counter-letter of 27 August 1981, indemnifying the IOR against loss on the letters of patronage
sources: deep-research dossier, synthesizing New York Times and Washington Post reporting on the Ambrosiano letters

stops.name: The Governatorato, archbishop and governor of the city
stops.date_confidence: Exact date attested (catholic-hierarchy.org). The title is corrected: Titular Archbishop of Horta and Pro-President of the Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State, not 'vice-president of the Governorate' as the research pool had it, the Governorate framing belonging to a later era. Coordinates corrected to the Palazzo del Governatorato; the pool's value sat 380 m west inside the Vatican Gardens.
stops.campa: John Paul II, three years into a pontificate consumed by Poland, promotes him twenty days after the letters of patronage are signed: Titular Archbishop of Horta, and Pro-President of the Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State, which makes him in practice the governor of the hundred and ten acres. He keeps the bank as well. The man who once cleared crowds ahead of Paul VI now has charge of the city's gendarmes, its post office, its museums, its gardens and its money.
suggested_refs: The Palazzo del Governatorato, seat of the Pontifical Commission for Vatican City State

stops.name: Vatican City, the guarantee reaffirmed
stops.date_confidence: The remark is dated to April 1982 by Christianity Today's September 1982 report, 'The Vatican Bank Scandal', where it is confirmed verbatim; the day is defaulted to 01. The Bank of Italy's long pressure on Calvi over the ownership of the offshore companies is attested in the general record of the affair.
stops.campa: Milan magistrates are already circling Ambrosiano, and the Bank of Italy has spent two years asking Calvi who actually owns the offshore companies. The answers are unsatisfactory and the questions do not stop. Ten weeks from this month Ambrosiano will be gone and Calvi dead in London, and every newspaper in Italy will print the sentence back at him. Asked in April whether the Vatican bank still stands behind the chairman of Ambrosiano, Marcinkus answers without hesitation and without qualification.
stops.quote: Roberto Calvi merits our trust. I know of no reason to doubt him.
stops.quote_source: Marcinkus, April 1982, quoted in Christianity Today, 'The Vatican Bank Scandal' (September 1982)
suggested_refs: Christianity Today, 'The Vatican Bank Scandal' (September 1982)

stops.name: The Institute for the Works of Religion, the bank goes down
stops.date_confidence: Calvi's letter of 5 June 1982 is attested; the quote is verbatim to 'gravest damage' in The Irish Examiner, 'Dirty money, dirtier tricks', corroborated by Wikipedia and murdermap.co.uk, and tagged [R] because it is an English translation and no facsimile of the Italian original was located. A trailing sentence circulating in search summaries is unattested and is not printed here. The collapse figure is reported between roughly $700 million and $1.5 billion; the dossier's $1.3 billion is one point in that range.
stops.campa: Calvi writes to John Paul II over Marcinkus's head, five days before he vanishes from his Rome apartment on a false passport. Ambrosiano fails owing somewhere between seven hundred million and one and a half billion dollars, and the letters of patronage surface. The central bank finds the hole, and the liquidators follow the Panamanian companies back to the tower behind St. Peter's. On the eighteenth of June Calvi is found hanging beneath a London bridge, bricks in his pockets and cash in his clothes.
stops.quote: Holiness, a possible collapse of the Ambrosiano Bank would provoke a catastrophe of unimaginable proportions in which the Church will suffer the gravest damage.
stops.quote_source: Roberto Calvi, letter to Pope John Paul II, 5 June 1982, as reproduced in The Irish Examiner, 'Dirty money, dirtier tricks'
suggested_refs: Blackfriars Bridge, London, where Calvi was found on 18 June 1982: his own stop, not this traveler's
The 2007 Rome trial in which five defendants were acquitted and the court ruled the death a murder
sources: The Irish Examiner, 'Dirty money, dirtier tricks'
Forbes, 'When The Apparent Suicide Of God's Banker Was Ruled A Murder'

stops.name: Vatican City, the archbishop answers the press
stops.date_confidence: The quote and Cardinal Benelli's remarks are confirmed verbatim in TIME, 'Italy: The Great Vatican Bank Mystery' (1982); TIME does not give a day, so the date is set to July 1982 with day defaulted to 01, to place the exchange after the June collapse. The dating within 1982 is inferred, not attested.
stops.campa: The Holy See's line is that the institute owes nothing: the companies were Calvi's, the letters were comfort, the losses are Italy's business. From inside the Curia, Cardinal Giovanni Benelli says publicly that being a friend of the pope is no reason to keep a post, and that if there was imprudence it came of incompetence and inexperience. Marcinkus does not resign and does not leave the walls. Reached by telephone in the tower, he speaks about himself in the third person.
stops.quote: The old archbishop is tranquil. His conscience is clear.
stops.quote_source: Marcinkus, quoted in TIME, 'Italy: The Great Vatican Bank Mystery' (1982)
suggested_refs: Cardinal Giovanni Benelli's criticism, TIME (1982): 'The fact that Archbishop Paul Marcinkus is a friend of the Pope's doesn't mean that he has to remain in the post.'
sources: TIME, 'Italy: The Great Vatican Bank Mystery' (1982)

stops.name: Vatican City, accused in print of a papal murder
stops.date_confidence: Publication attested (Wikipedia, 'In God's Name'; Jonathan Cape / Bantam, 1984); month and day defaulted to 01. The murder allegation itself is [R] and unsubstantiated, refuted by John Cornwell, 'A Thief in the Night' (1989). The stop sits at Marcinkus's own pin because the book is an event in his life and not a place he went: Yallop's own travels and John Paul I's death belong to their own files.
stops.campa: David Yallop publishes In God's Name, which argues that John Paul I was murdered in 1978 to stop him cleaning out Vatican finance, and names Marcinkus among the men with a motive. It sells in the millions and is translated into more than a dozen languages. No inquiry and no historian has produced evidence for any of it, and John Cornwell's investigation five years later takes the charge apart in detail. The book remains in print as a mass-market paperback.
suggested_refs: David Yallop, In God's Name (1984)
John Cornwell, A Thief in the Night (1989), the principal rebuttal
sources: John Cornwell, A Thief in the Night (1989)

stops.name: Geneva, the Vatican pays the creditors
stops.date_confidence: Date corrected and refined from the pool's '1984-05': UPI reports the accord initialled on the Sunday and signed at Geneva on Friday 25 May 1984. The amounts are contested and both are reported: $250 million from the IOR within a settlement above $500 million, of which $244 million went to 120 creditor banks (UPI), against a figure of $224 million in Wikipedia's Calvi article. The attested phrase is 'in recognition of moral involvement'; the pool's 'in a spirit of reciprocity' is not attested anywhere located and is not used. City-level pin; the meeting venue is [R].
stops.campa: Italy's Treasury has pressed for a settlement for two years. On the twenty-fifth of May the Vatican negotiators and the creditor banks sign in Geneva. The Institute for the Works of Religion pays two hundred and fifty million dollars into an accord worth more than five hundred million, of which two hundred and forty-four million goes to a hundred and twenty banks. The money is paid in recognition of moral involvement, and admits no legal liability. Other accounts put the institute's share at two hundred and twenty-four million, and the difference has never been reconciled.
